***

# A Historical Pivot: France Returns to NATO’s Military Command After 43 Years

In March 2009, French foreign policy underwent its most significant transformation in half a century. President Nicolas Sarkozy successfully navigated a fierce political storm to orchestrate France’s full return to NATO’s integrated military command structure. Ending a 43-year self-imposed absence from the Alliance’s central decision-making apparatus, the move marked a decisive break with decades of entrenched strategic tradition and reshaped the balance of transatlantic relations.

### The Shadow of De Gaulle

To understand the weight of Sarkozy’s initiative, one must look back to 1966. In a move that shocked the Western world, President Charles de Gaulle withdrew France from NATO’s integrated military command—though not from the political alliance itself—and ordered foreign NATO bases off French soil. De Gaulle argued that the arrangement compromised French sovereignty and effectively forced France to subvert its defense decisions to the strategic priorities of the United States.

For the next four decades, "Gaullism"—a doctrine emphasizing absolute national independence, a distinct strategic distance from Washington, and the primacy of France's independent nuclear deterrent (*force de frappe*)—became an untouchable pillar of French diplomacy. Consecutive presidents, both from the left and the right, maintained this status quo. France remained a reliable ally, participating in NATO missions in the Balkans and Afghanistan, but it firmly refused to reintegrate into the high-level military planning councils.

### Sarkozy’s Case for Realism

Upon taking office in 2007, President Nicolas Sarkozy viewed this long-standing policy as an outdated paradox. His argument was fundamentally pragmatic: France was already sending thousands of troops to risk their lives in NATO-led operations, making it one of the largest contributors of manpower and funding to the alliance. Yet, because it sat outside the military command structure, Paris had virtually no say in drafting overall alliance strategy, setting operational targets, or assigning high-level command positions. 

"We are paying, we are sending troops, but we are not participating in the committees that decide on their operational objectives," Sarkozy argued. 

Furthermore, Sarkozy contended that a fully integrated France could act as a catalyst for a stronger, more autonomous European Union defense structure. By reassuring Washington of France’s commitment to NATO, he aimed to dismantle American skepticism toward European defense initiatives.

### A Fiery Political Backlash

Sarkozy’s ambition met fierce resistance across the French political spectrum. The proposal ignited a passionate debate about national identity, strategic autonomy, and France's role in the global order.

On the left, the Opposition Socialist Party, led by figures like François Hollande, accused Sarkozy of an act of strategic alignment with the United States. Coming just six years after the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq—which France had famously opposed at the United Nations—critics warned that rejoining NATO’s command structure would drag France into unwanted foreign conflicts and strip the country of its role as an independent voice on the world stage.

Resistance was equally intense on the right. Old-guard Gaullists within Sarkozy’s own party, the Union for a Popular Movement (UMP), along with former Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin, denounced the move as a betrayal of France’s heritage and a unnecessary surrender of sovereignty. Critics labeled Sarkozy "Sarko the American," accusing him of subservience to Washington.

### The Parliamentary Showdown

Facing mounting pressure, Sarkozy opted to make the vote in the National Assembly a matter of confidence in his government’s broader foreign policy. 

The debate in the National Assembly on March 17, 2009, was charged with historic weight. Prime Minister François Fillon defended the proposal before a tense chamber, arguing that remaining partially outside NATO was a self-imposed handicap that diminished French influence rather than preserving it.

When the votes were tallied, the government prevailed. The National Assembly approved the return to NATO’s integrated command by a vote of 329 to 238. Sarkozy had secured his victory, backed predominantly by his center-right parliamentary majority, while overcoming a nearly unified opposition.

### A New Era in Transatlantic Defense

The historic vote paved the way for France’s formal return to the fold at NATO’s 60th-anniversary summit in Strasbourg and Kehl in April 2009. In exchange for its full reintegration, France secured major leadership roles, including the post of Supreme Allied Commander Transformation in Norfolk, Virginia—one of NATO's two strategic commands.

By closing the 43-year rift, France reclaimed a seat at the top table of Western military strategy. While critics continued to debate the long-term impact on French diplomacy, the 2009 vote undeniably reshaped the geopolitics of the post-Cold War era, solidifying France’s place at the core of transatlantic security while preserving its independent nuclear capability.

**PARIS (CNN)** — In a landmark vote that reshapes European security and overturns decades of diplomatic orthodoxy, France’s National Assembly voted Tuesday to rejoin NATO’s integrated military command, bringing a formal end to a 43-year rift with the Western alliance.

Lawmakers in the lower house of parliament backed President Nicolas Sarkozy’s controversial shift by a vote of 329 to 238, clearing the way for Paris to take a full seat at NATO's military leadership table ahead of the alliance’s 60th-anniversary summit next month.

The high-stakes vote, framed as a motion of confidence in the government of Prime Minister François Fillon, caps weeks of fierce debate over France’s identity on the global stage. 

"The time has come to end this situation," Fillon told lawmakers before the vote. "France must be where decisions are made, not where they are suffered."

### The Ghost of de Gaulle

The decision dismantles one of the most sacred tenets of modern French foreign policy, established in 1966 by post-war hero and President General Charles de Gaulle. 

At the height of the Cold War, de Gaulle dramatically withdrew France from NATO’s integrated military command—though not the political alliance itself—in a fierce assertion of French national sovereignty. Driven by a desire to avoid being dragged into conflicts dictated by the United States, de Gaulle ordered foreign NATO troops off French soil and forced the alliance to move its headquarters from Paris to Brussels.

For over four decades, "Gaullism"—the belief in a fiercely independent, non-aligned France capable of acting as a bridge between superpowers—served as the unquestioned bedrock of French diplomacy under leaders from both the left and right.

### Sarkozy’s Calculus: "An Ally, Not a Vassal"

President Sarkozy, an openly pro-American conservative who earned the moniker "Sarkozy the American" during his 2007 election campaign, has spent months arguing that de Gaulle’s 1966 policy is an outdated relic of the Cold War.

Sarkozy’s government argued that France was already suffering the costs of NATO involvement without reaping the strategic benefits. France is currently the fourth-largest troop contributor to NATO missions, with thousands of soldiers deployed in Afghanistan and the Balkans. Yet, because of its self-imposed exile from the military command, French generals have been excluded from top-level operational planning.

"We are sending our soldiers into the field, but we are not in the rooms where the maps are drawn," Sarkozy said in a speech last week. "Rejoining the command makes France stronger, not weaker. A nation that is independent is a nation that acts. We will be an ally, not a vassal."

Under the new arrangement, France is expected to secure two major NATO command posts, including a strategic command center in Norfolk, Virginia. Sarkozy has maintained that France will retain complete control over its nuclear deterrent and will not place French troops under permanent peacetime NATO command.

### Fierce Domestic Backlash

Despite the government's victory, the move has triggered a political firestorm in Paris, uniting an unyielding opposition of Socialists, Communists, and hardline Gaullists within Sarkozy’s own party who accuse the president of betraying national pride.

Socialist leader François Hollande condemned the vote as a submission to Washington.

"This is a fundamental error," Hollande said during the debate. "You are aligning France with American strategy at a time when the world needs an independent voice. You are exchanging our freedom of tone for a few general staff posts."

Critics also argue that the move undermines efforts to build an independent European Union defense force, placing Europe’s security apparatus firmly back under American oversight.

### A New Era for the Alliance

In Washington and Brussels, the vote has been greeted with quiet enthusiasm. Officials in the Obama administration view France’s full return as a vital step toward revitalizing the 28-nation alliance as it faces complex global threats, including the war in Afghanistan, international piracy, and cyber warfare.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates praised the decision, calling France a "pivotal power" whose full participation in NATO is long overdue.

The formal reintegration will be finalized on April 3–4, when Sarkozy co-hosts NATO’s 60th-anniversary summit alongside German Chancellor Angela Merkel, bridging the Rhine at Strasbourg and Kehl. 

Forty-three years after Charles de Gaulle famously handed NATO its eviction notice, France is coming home—and bringing a new vision for Western defense with it.

President Nicolas Sarkozy’s decisive push to bring Paris back into the heart of the transatlantic alliance was solidified following a dramatic vote of confidence in the French National Assembly, overcoming fierce resistance from both political opponents and traditionalists within his own party.

The historic shift, finalized ahead of NATO’s 60th-anniversary summit in Strasbourg and Kehl, marks the formal end of a doctrine established in 1966 by General Charles de Gaulle. De Gaulle had famously withdrawn France from NATO’s military command to preserve national sovereignty and protest what he viewed as American hegemony within the alliance.

"The time has come to put an end to this situation," President Sarkozy declared during a keynote speech at the École Militaire in Paris. "A nation that is not present at the table where decisions are made is not an independent nation. By returning fully to NATO, France will be stronger, and Europe will be stronger."

---

### **Ending a 43-Year Anomaly**

While France was a founding member of NATO in 1949, De Gaulle’s 1966 decision forced NATO to move its headquarters from Paris to Brussels and expelled foreign military bases from French soil. France remained a member of NATO’s political alliance and retained its seat on the North Atlantic Council, but its armed forces operated strictly outside the unified military command structure.

Over the past two decades, however, that separation had become increasingly symbolic. French forces have actively fought alongside NATO troops in major operations, including the Balkans in the 1990s and the ongoing mission in Afghanistan. 

Sarkozy argued that the legacy arrangement had left France in an absurd position: contributing the fifth-largest number of troops to NATO operations while having zero say in top-level military strategy and planning. Under the new arrangement, French officers will assume senior leadership roles within NATO's command hierarchy, including heading the Strategic Allied Command Transformation in Norfolk, Virginia, and the Joint Command in Lisbon.

---

### **A Political Firestorm in Paris**

Despite the pragmatic rationale offered by the Élysée Palace, the decision ignited a political firestorm across France, striking at the core of French national identity and diplomatic tradition.

Critics from across the political spectrum accused Sarkozy of betraying the fundamental tenets of "Gaullism"—the doctrine of strategic independence, non-alignment, and a distinct French voice in global affairs.

Socialist Party leader François Hollande spearheaded the opposition in Parliament, launching a motion of censure against the government. "Rejoining the military command means placing French diplomacy under American guardianship," Hollande warned during a heated parliamentary debate. "It deprives France of its unique role as a mediator between powers."

Resistance was equally potent on the political right. Former Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin, a prominent neo-Gaullist, publicly condemned the decision, arguing that France was surrendering its geopolitical singularity for little in return. Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Front similarly denounced the move as an act of "vassalage" to Washington.

Ultimately, Prime Minister François Fillon’s government survived the no-confidence vote by a margin of 329 to 238, clearing the final domestic hurdle for France's full return.

---

### **Reactions from Washington and Brussels**

The response from Western capitals has been overwhelmingly positive. US President Barack Obama’s administration warmly welcomed Paris's decision, viewing it as a vital step toward reinvigorating transatlantic relations after years of tension over the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

NATO Secretary General Jaap de Hoop Scheffer called the move a "historic step forward," stating that full French participation would make the alliance stronger, more dynamic, and better equipped to handle 21st-century security threats.

The move is also expected to reshape European defense dynamics. For years, Central and Eastern European nations had been wary of French efforts to build an independent European Union defense system, fearing it would undermine NATO. By fully re-integrating into NATO, France hopes to reassure its Eastern allies while convincing them that a stronger European defense strategy can complement, rather than compete with, the alliance.

---

### **Red Lines and Nuclear Autonomy**

Addressing concerns that France’s strategic autonomy would be eroded, French officials emphasized that strict "red lines" had been maintained.

Under the terms of the re-integration:
* **Nuclear Deterrent:** France’s independent nuclear force (*Force de Frappe*) will remain entirely outside NATO command, maintaining absolute national control.
* **Troop Deployment:** No French troops will be placed under permanent NATO command during peacetime. France retains the exclusive power to decide when, where, and how its military forces are deployed.

---

### **A New Era for Transatlantic Security**

As leaders gather for the Strasbourg-Kehl summit, the image of French, American, and European leaders standing united marks a profound symbolic shift. 

By closing the book on a 43-year rift, President Sarkozy has bet that France can exert greater influence on world affairs from within NATO’s command room than from the outside. Whether this move will truly give Paris a stronger leverage over US foreign policy—or ultimately submerge French diplomacy into a broader Western consensus—remains the central question facing France's new strategic posture.

At the height of the Cold War, De Gaulle dramatically pulled France out of NATO’s military structure—though remaining part of its political alliance—in an assertion of national sovereignty. The historic move forced Allied Supreme Headquarters to pack up and leave French soil for Brussels, while cementing the "Gaullist" doctrine of strategic autonomy and nuclear independence as a sacred consensus across the French political spectrum.

**PARIS** — March 17, 2009

### French Assembly Backs Sarkozy’s Historic Return to NATO Military Command

**By Jean-Luc Martin and Sarah Jenkins**

In a historic vote that redrafts the contours of European security and upends four decades of diplomatic tradition, the French National Assembly on Tuesday formally endorsed President Nicolas Sarkozy’s plan to fully reintegrate France into NATO’s integrated military command structure. 

Following days of passionate, sometimes furious debate in the Palais Bourbon, the center-right government of Prime Minister François Fillon comfortably defeated a motion of no confidence brought by the Socialist opposition. The final vote of 329 to 238 cements France’s return to the alliance’s core decision-making bodies, ending a 43-year rift that began when General Charles de Gaulle abruptly pulled French forces out of NATO command in 1966.

The decision clears the way for President Sarkozy to formally announce the full return at NATO’s 60th anniversary summit in Strasbourg and Kehl next month.

#### A Fractured Legacy: The Debate over Independence

For decades, Gaullist dogma dictated that France maintain a unique, non-aligned posture within the Western coalition—remaining a full political member of NATO while keeping its armed forces, including its nuclear deterrent, strictly under sovereign national command. 

Addressing the Assembly ahead of the vote, Prime Minister Fillon argued that the world had fundamentally changed since the height of the Cold War and that France’s strategic isolation was no longer serving its national interests.

"The time for nostalgia is over," Mr. Fillon declared to a noisy chamber. "France remains a free nation, an independent power, an ally that chooses its destinies. But how can we pretend to influence NATO’s strategy if we are not in the rooms where that strategy is planned?"

President Sarkozy, who made the return to NATO a cornerstone of his foreign policy overhaul, has repeatedly insisted that being a loyal ally does not mean becoming a "vassal" of Washington. He argued that despite being out of the command structure, France was already the fifth-largest contributor of troops to NATO operations, including missions in Afghanistan and the Balkans, yet lacked the structural clout to shape high-level military planning.

Furthermore, Mr. Sarkozy framed the move as a prerequisite for strengthening a complementary European Union defense initiative—a long-held ambition of Paris that had historically met with skepticism from Washington and pro-NATO European partners.

#### Fierce Pushback from Left and Right

The proposed realignment touched a raw nerve across the French political spectrum, provoking an intense debate over national identity, sovereignty, and the legacy of De Gaulle.

Socialist Party leader François Hollande spearheaded the opposition, accusing the president of surrendering France’s distinct diplomatic voice on the world stage. Critics argued that a fully integrated France would inevitably be dragged into American-led foreign policy misadventures, pointing to France's vocal opposition to the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq as a prime example of the value of strategic independence.

"Reintegrating into the military command means aligning ourselves with American policy," Mr. Hollande warned during the debate. "It deprives France of its singularity, its posture as a mediator, and its freedom of tone which gave it such weight in global affairs."

Opposition was not confined to the Left. A faction of traditional Gaullists within Mr. Sarkozy’s own party, the Union for a Popular Movement (UMP), expressed deep reservations. Former Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin, a staunch defender of the 1966 legacy, publicly condemned the move as an "unnecessary alignment" that offered no clear strategic gain in exchange for a loss of prestige.

"France is not a nation like any other," Mr. de Villepin said in a statement preceding the vote. "Our strength lies in our ability to say 'no' when our allies are wrong."

#### Looking to the Summit

Despite the political theater in Paris, public interest in the vote remained moderate, with polls showing the French electorate largely divided or indifferent to the technicalities of military integration. 

U.S. and NATO officials have warmly welcomed the outcome. Pentagon officials noted that France's full participation will streamline joint operations and elevate French officers into top leadership roles at NATO command posts in Norfolk, Virginia, and Allied Command Operations in Mons, Belgium.

As the debate in the Assembly drew to a close late Tuesday night, Defense Minister Hervé Morin sought to reassure both the public and parliamentarians that France's independent nuclear force would remain entirely outside NATO control. 

"France is returning to its rightful place," Mr. Morin said. "Not to submit, but to lead."
